Open Day · Waterloo · November 2026 · Report

Intelligent Agents for Software Engineering

Agentic software engineering and its challenges

Agentic software engineering hands parts of the software lifecycle to AI agents that plan, write, test and repair code with little human help. This report sets out how such agents work and where they stand against a human software engineer, and then examines the 4 challenges that decide whether the approach holds up on real projects: how many agents are orchestrated on one project, how an agent obtains and keeps a mental model of the software it works on, how that project knowledge is structured as a graph and shared by many agents, and how an agent learns from its own mistakes. For each, it states the problem, describes how current systems address it, summarizes what published research shows, and identifies what remains open.

A graph store of project knowledge, shared by many agents— Artifact Graph turns the artifacts of spec-driven development into a graph that agents can query and update safely.

01 · Agents

What an agent is

A language model in a loop: it reads, decides, acts with a tool, observes the result, and repeats.

The model underneath

An agent is built on a large language model (LLM). The model reads a prompt, splits it into tokens (words or word pieces), [1] turns each token into a vector of numbers (an embedding), and passes the vectors through a stack of transformer blocks. Each block combines a self-attention layer, which relates every token to the others, with a feed-forward network, wrapped in normalization and residual connections, and a model may have dozens or hundreds of such blocks. [2] A final layer gives a probability to every possible next token. The model picks one, appends it to the text, and runs the whole process again, one token at a time, until the response is complete. GPT-3 is an autoregressive model of this kind, with 175 billion parameters. [3]

What it is

An agent is a language model that works in a loop. It starts from a task, builds its context (its instructions, what it remembers, and everything that has happened so far), reasons about the next step, and then either calls a tool or finishes. The result of each tool call comes back as an observation and becomes part of the next round. [4][5]

The problem

A chatbot answers once and stops. Real work, such as fixing a bug in a large repository, needs exploring, trying something, and checking the result. That is only possible if the model can act and see what its actions did.

How it works

7 steps: the task; build the context; the model reasons; choose an action; run a tool in the environment (for a coding agent, the project files and a terminal); observe the output; stop and report when the task is finished or a limit, such as a maximum number of steps, is reached. Anthropic describes the same loop for Claude Code as gather context, take action, verify the result, and repeat. [6]

Around the loop sit the model itself, the instructions, the tools, the memory, the environment and the stop rule. A survey of agent research describes the same parts as a profile, a memory, planning and action. [7]

What research says

ReAct showed that interleaving reasoning with actions lets the model plan, track and update what it is doing. [4] SWE-agent showed that tools designed for the agent, rather than for a human, change the result. [8] Anthropic separates workflows, where code decides the path, from agents, where the model directs its own process. [5] OpenHands is an open platform that runs agent actions in a sandbox and returns observations. [9]

Why it matters here

Everything else in this report connects, extends or improves these parts: many agents working together (orchestration), a memory that lasts across sessions (the mental model), and a loop that improves the parts themselves (self-evolution).

02 · Software Factory

From software engineer to coding agent

The lifecycle is the same; today humans do every stage, and a team of agents could do them tomorrow.

What it is

The Vee model, introduced to systems engineering by Mooz and Forsberg in 1991, runs from user needs at the upper left to a user-validated system at the upper right. [10] Going down the left side, needs become requirements, then a system design, then a detailed design, and at the bottom the code is written. Going up the right side, units are tested, then integrated, then the whole system is verified, and finally accepted and deployed. In the usual software form of the model each design level has a matching test level, and the check is planned when the design is made.

The problem

Coding is only part of an engineer's job. Studies of developers' working days find that they spend little of their time on development itself. [11] A coding agent that only writes code covers a small part of the V.

Who does what

Today, humans fill every box: an analyst, an architect, a developer, a tester, a quality engineer and a release engineer. The vision is a team with one agent per stage (requirements, design, coding, test, verification, deployment), each checking the work of the others, as the V asks.

Where agents are today

Our reading of the published benchmarks is that agents are furthest along at coding and least along at the ends of the V. SWE-Lancer offers more than 1,400 real freelance tasks, and its authors report that frontier models still fail to solve most of them. [12] A benchmark that covers the whole lifecycle, from design to acceptance testing, finds that current models fail to solve it. [13] For operations, a benchmark of build, monitoring and issue tasks reports that agents struggle with monitoring and build configuration. [14] Work on agents that elicit requirements is, to our reading, still at the research-prototype stage.

Why it matters here

One super-agent is not enough. The gap between coding and the rest of the lifecycle is the reason we study teams of agents, and how to run them.

03 · Orchestration

Many agents, one project

Work is split into a graph of tasks, built in parallel, and checked before it reaches the main branch.

What it is

An orchestrator reads the goal and turns it into tasks. A planner makes one plan and sizes the work so that each part fits one worker. Workers then run at the same time, each on its own branch, so they cannot overwrite each other. A tester agent, separate from the worker that wrote the code, checks each branch against the specification, and only a branch that passes is merged into main by an integrator. This is an orchestrator-worker pattern, a lead agent that coordinates specialised workers. [15]

The problem

One agent working alone is slow and loses track of a large project. But more agents is not always better. Anthropic reports that multi-agent systems use about 15 times the tokens of a chat, and agents alone about 4 times, and notes that most coding tasks have fewer truly parallel parts than research tasks. [15] A study of 260 agent configurations on 6 benchmarks found results from about 81% better to 70% worse than a single agent, depending on whether the task splits cleanly or must be done in order. [16]

How the split works

First a skeleton defines every name that more than one part will use, and the main path through the program. Then the rest of the work becomes slices that start from the skeleton and run side by side. A slice waits for another only when it cannot be tested without it. The graph is kept wide and shallow. Each slice has its own tester, and only tested work reaches main.

What research says

Recent coding work uses the same shape: workers in isolated git worktrees, a dependency-aware plan, and test-based verification before merging. On PaperBench and Commit0 this beat a single agent by 25.6 and 14.7 points. [17] Role-based teams were explored earlier by MetaGPT and ChatDev. [18][19] How the work is split matters: giving one agent to each file raised cost by 44% and 60% on 2 benchmarks for small gains, while splitting along the dependency graph improved the pass rate by up to 14 points, was up to 2.1 times faster, and cost up to 35% less. [20] (Python only, one model, 28 tasks.)

A real run

Our system, Software Factory, built a Python command-line library from a specification of about 2,000 lines. The orchestrator first split the specification into 9 areas and, within 3 minutes, created 53 issues, so work started in every area at once. Things went wrong and were handled: a planner hit its output limit twice and the orchestrator re-planned; 3 agents hit the same gap in the specification and one planner decided; a merge that did not happen was caught and done for real; a swapped branch was blocked and re-routed. The run used 150 agents over 2 h 46 min and cost $7.79. It produced 44 merges, and all 17 defects that testers found were fixed. On the hidden tests it passed 30 of 70, so there is more to do.

04 · Mental model

What an engineer remembers, and an agent forgets

A good engineer keeps more than code in mind. An agent needs a persistent mental model to do the same.

What it is

The idea is old. Kenneth Craik suggested in 1943 that the mind carries small-scale models of reality and uses them to try out options before acting. [21] Edward Tolman showed in 1948 that animals form cognitive maps. [22] Philip Johnson-Laird described mental models built from experience and held in working memory in 1983. [23] In software, research on developer work habits finds that developers create and maintain rich mental models of the code. [24] Expert engineers hold the components, how they depend on each other, the architecture, the reasons for decisions, the constraints and past choices: a map far richer than the source code.

The problem

The code says what the system does; the hardest questions are about why. Why was it written this way? What else was tried? What breaks if I change it? That knowledge is fuzzy ("I know it works but cannot say why"), personal (hard to hand over) and silent (pitfalls live only with whoever hit them), so it leaves when people do.

Agents have this problem in the extreme. A coding agent is stateless: in one session it explores the repository, finds a root cause, learns the code patterns and makes a design decision, and when the session ends the context window is cleared. The next session starts almost empty and repeats the exploration. The window is also limited in size; MemGPT treats this like a computer's memory, with a small fast memory and a larger slower one that the agent manages. [25]

How the Mental Model works

The Mental Model is a persistent, cross-session knowledge store for coding agents, outside the context window. It is structured and typed: architecture and structure, decisions and rationale, constraints, pitfalls and learnings, patterns, and experiment history. It is grounded in the task, the codebase and the agent's reasoning, not in the code text itself. It acts as a teacher (the agent asks it why something was done) and as a hand-off between agents: one agent writes its discoveries, another builds on them. A retrieval step decides when knowledge is delivered, how much, and how relevant it is.

What research says

Surveys describe memory as the key component for agents that interact with an environment over time. [26] For coding agents, a study of memory built from earlier subtasks reports a mean gain of 4.7 points in Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified (6.8 points on Gemini 2.5 Pro); this memory comes from subtasks rather than strictly across sessions. [27]

Open questions

What to store, when to retrieve it, and how to keep it correct as the code changes are still open. A memory that is wrong or too large is worse than none.

05 · Artifact Graph

A graph store of project knowledge, shared by many agents

Artifact Graph turns the artifacts of spec-driven development into a graph that agents can query and update safely.

What it is

Artifact Graph is a database-like layer for the artifacts of spec-driven development: requirements, designs, decisions, tasks and scenarios. The documents stay the source of truth. Artifact Graph projects their content into typed nodes and typed relationships (a change contains a specification and a design, a specification defines requirements, a requirement is evidenced by a scenario, a design records decisions, risks and tasks), each traced back to its source. Relationships nobody wrote down are inferred, with a confidence and a rationale, and are not treated as proof. [28][29][30]

The problem

More project knowledge does not give better context. One change adds requirements, designs, decisions, tasks and scenarios, and the pool grows faster than a prompt can hold. Loading everything hands the filtering problem to the model, and critical constraints get buried. [31]

How retrieval works

Artifact Graph retrieves the smallest sufficient context. The task is split into information needs; semantic search finds the entry nodes even when the wording differs; graph edges recover dependencies, constraints, decisions and history; and the result is revealed progressively, core first, then related items, then evidence, only where reasoning shows a gap. [28][32]

Many agents, one graph

When several agents edit the knowledge at once, updates are staged. An agent's change becomes a candidate set of nodes and edges kept out of shared retrieval, is inspected for structure, consistency, conflicts and traceability, and is committed as one logical update, with earlier versions kept. A conflicting change is held for review. [33][34]

Evidence and limits

On 16 SlopCodeBench problems, Artifact Graph (v1.2.0) used 26.8% less context (lower on 16 of 16 problems), 14.2% less cost (16 of 16) and 9.2% fewer tokens (14 of 16) per checkpoint than an OpenSpec-only baseline. The quality differences were small and every interval crossed zero, so they are not conclusive. Artifact Graph does not scan the repository, index source code or guarantee that artifacts are correct; tests and review still matter. [35]

06 · Self-evolution

Learning from mistakes

The agent reviews what went wrong, writes the lesson down, uses it next time, and in the strongest form improves itself.

What it is

Self-evolution has 2 loops. In the inner loop the agent acts, we evaluate the result with tests and review, the agent reflects on why it failed, writes the lesson down, and stores it in memory for the next try. In the outer loop the agent changes itself: its own tools, prompts, and even its own code. Surveys describe the general loop as inputs, the agent, its environment, and an optimizer that updates the agent from feedback. [36]

The problem

Until now the agent follows rules we wrote. Language models themselves stay fixed after training, so improvement has to come from what surrounds them: memory, skills, prompts, tools and code.

How it works

Inner loop: Reflexion keeps the agent's own written reflections in an episodic memory buffer. [37] Voyager saves working solutions as an ever-growing library of executable skills (in Minecraft, not in coding). [38] ExpeL gathers experience and turns it into natural-language knowledge, with no change to the model's weights. [39]

Outer loop: the Self-Improving Coding Agent edits its own code. [40] The Darwin Godel Machine keeps an archive of agents, lets them modify themselves, and tests each change on coding benchmarks. [41] In both, a change is kept only if the benchmark score does not drop.

What research says

Reflexion reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, against 80% for GPT-4 at the time. [37] The Self-Improving Coding Agent raised its score from 17% to 53% on a random subset of SWE-bench Verified. [40] The Darwin Godel Machine improved from 20.0% to 50.0% on SWE-bench and from 14.2% to 30.7% on Polyglot. [41] These are different benchmarks, so compare within a paper, not across.

Risks

Optimizing only for a benchmark can introduce vulnerabilities, as the Darwin Godel Machine authors note, and their experiments ran with sandboxing and human oversight. [41] An agent may also learn to game the test, drift, or forget earlier skills. That is why the test gate and a human stay in the loop.

07 · Challenges

4 challenges ahead

Orchestration

How must orchestration happen?

  • Split along the dependency graph. A skeleton first, then slices that run side by side and wait only where a test needs another slice. Not by file, and not by line count.[20]
  • Isolate and check every branch. A separate tester sits between each worker and main; merge only after it passes.[17]
  • Add agents only where the task splits cleanly. A multi-agent system can use about 15 times the tokens of a chat, and tasks that must be done in order can get much worse.[15][16]

Mental model

How must a mental model be made, and how must it help?

  • Store what the code cannot say. Architecture, decisions and their reasons, constraints, pitfalls, patterns and history, typed and scoped, outside the context window.
  • Deliver the right knowledge at the right time. Decide when it is retrieved and how much, so the context stays small.[25][28]
  • Pass it on, and keep it correct. Share it between sessions and agents so nothing is rediscovered, and keep it right as the code changes. This last part is still an open problem.[27][33]

Artifact Graph

How must project knowledge be structured and shared?

  • Make the knowledge a graph of typed records. Requirements, designs, decisions, tasks and scenarios become typed nodes and edges, each traced to its source document. Inferred links carry a confidence and are not proof.[28][29]
  • Retrieve the smallest sufficient context. Find entry points by meaning, follow edges to dependencies and constraints, and reveal more only where reasoning shows a gap.[31][32]
  • Let many agents update it safely. Stage each change, inspect it for structure, conflicts and traceability, commit it as one update, and hold conflicting changes for review.[33][34]

Self-evolution

How must self-evolution work?

  • Learn in an inner loop. Reflect on each failure, write the lesson down, store it, and reuse it.[37][39]
  • Change itself only through a test gate. Keep a change only if the benchmark score does not drop.[40][41]
  • Keep a sandbox and a human in the loop. Optimizing only for a benchmark can introduce vulnerabilities.[41]
